razors.name: 25-plus razor
razors.summary: Avoid dismissing unfamiliar technologies solely because younger people value them.
razors.body: Unfamiliarity can masquerade as informed criticism. The age label is rhetorical and does not identify a scientifically established threshold. The age cutoff is arbitrary advice, not a scientific threshold.
razors.lensQuestion: Am I evaluating this unfamiliar trend by its actual merits or by discomfort with a younger audience?

examples.text: An older manager rejects a new communication format before examining how clients use it.
examples.note: Investigating the use case is more informative than treating either age group as automatically right.

limitations: The age cutoff is arbitrary advice, not a scientific threshold.

razors.name: Alder's razor
razors.summary: Restrict debate to questions that observation or experiment can settle.
razors.body: The rule narrows a method of inquiry rather than settling every worthwhile question. Ethics, mathematics, and conceptual analysis cannot simply be dismissed because they are not experiments. A contestable methodological stance; not a theorem about meaning or value.
razors.lensQuestion: Which observation could distinguish the competing claims?

examples.text: Two accounts say the world has different invisible causes, but stipulate identical observable consequences forever.
examples.note: There is no proposed empirical test between them. Alder's stance would set this empirical debate aside.

limitations: A contestable methodological stance; not a theorem about meaning or value.

razors.name: Boredom razor
razors.summary: Stepping away from stimulation can provide space to reconsider a problem.
razors.body: Periods without new stimulation can give room for reflection. Restlessness does not guarantee insight, and some problems require new information rather than incubation. Context-dependent advice.
razors.lensQuestion: Would stepping away from constant input help me reconsider the problem?

examples.text: After repeatedly rereading an unproductive draft, a writer takes a quiet walk before revising.
examples.note: The pause may permit a new perspective, but it does not replace the later work of checking the draft.

limitations: Context-dependent advice.

razors.name: Bragging razor
razors.summary: Check self-promotional claims before relying on them.
razors.body:
When someone praises their own skills or results, check what supports the claim before relying on it. They may describe their best result while leaving out failures, help from others, or a longer run of ordinary results. Even an accurate success story can give an incomplete picture.

Look for evidence that someone else can check, such as a complete record, work samples, or confirmation from people involved. Give more weight to evidence that supports the specific claim than to confidence, status, or an impressive story.
razors.lensQuestion: How could someone else check this claim?

examples.text: A consultant says they doubled a client's sales. The only support is a glowing testimonial with no figures or dates.
examples.note: The testimonial shows customer approval, but it does not establish how much sales changed or what caused the change.

limitations: A person may be unable to disclose private records; other evidence can still support the claim.
An unverified claim can be true. Missing support leaves uncertainty rather than establishing falsehood.

razors.name: Charisma razor
razors.summary: Evaluate the argument separately from the speaker's charm.
razors.body: Delivery can change perceived credibility independently of evidence. The opposite appearance, awkwardness, is also not a reliable signal of truth. Lack of charisma also does not establish credibility.
razors.lensQuestion: Would I accept the same argument in writing without this speaker's delivery?

examples.text: A polished presenter offers an investment claim with no supporting data.
examples.note: Removing the performance leaves an evidential gap that charm cannot fill.

limitations: Lack of charisma also does not establish credibility.

razors.name: Chatton's anti-razor
razors.summary: Add explanatory resources when fewer resources cannot account for what must be explained.
razors.body: Necessary complexity is not an offense against parsimony. The additional entity or mechanism still needs justification rather than being introduced merely to save a favored theory. A counterweight to excessive parsimony.
razors.lensQuestion: Have explanatory resources been removed even though the remaining account cannot explain the facts?

examples.text: One mechanism explains a machine's overheating, but a separate electrical fault explains its intermittent shutdowns.
examples.note: A second mechanism is warranted if the one-cause account cannot explain both observations.

limitations: A counterweight to excessive parsimony.

razors.name: Discomfort razor
razors.summary: Do not automatically reject opportunities because they involve discomfort.
razors.body: Some useful activities are initially uncomfortable because they are unfamiliar. Discomfort alone does not distinguish development from injury or exploitation. Discomfort does not by itself establish growth or benefit.
razors.lensQuestion: Is this discomfort a manageable cost of learning or a signal of genuine harm?

examples.text: A novice avoids asking any questions because speaking in a study group feels awkward.
examples.note: The awkwardness may be a manageable obstacle to learning; dangerous or degrading treatment would be different.

limitations: Discomfort does not by itself establish growth or benefit.

razors.name: Early–late razor
razors.summary: Different communities may reflect different adoption stages.
razors.body: Different communities can encounter innovations at different times. Platform stereotypes and timing rules can become obsolete quickly. Platform-specific timing claims are unstable generalizations.
razors.lensQuestion: Does this community provide evidence about adoption timing relevant to my actual audience?

examples.text: A niche forum discusses a product long before it appears in a mainstream trade publication.
examples.note: This may indicate different audiences, but the platform alone cannot establish future adoption.

limitations: Platform-specific timing claims are unstable generalizations.

razors.name: Einstein's razor
razors.summary: Simplify an account as far as possible while preserving necessary adequacy.
razors.body: Simplicity is constrained by what an account must explain. Removing complexity that carries necessary information defeats the purpose of simplification. The familiar slogan is a paraphrase with uncertain exact attribution.
razors.lensQuestion: What can be removed without losing explanatory or predictive adequacy?

examples.text: A useful model needs temperature and pressure, but a shorter model discards pressure and misses known outcomes.
examples.note: The shorter model is too simple for the task, despite containing fewer variables.

limitations: The familiar slogan is a paraphrase with uncertain exact attribution.

razors.name: Elon's razor
razors.summary: The most entertaining outcome is supposedly the most likely.
razors.body: The saying treats entertainment as if it predicted outcomes. It is best understood as playful speculation rather than a reliable guide to belief. A playful conjecture; no established probability principle supports it.
razors.lensQuestion: Am I confusing an entertaining story with a well-supported forecast?

examples.text: A dramatic corporate reversal is judged likely because it would make a compelling film.
examples.note: Narrative appeal supplies no probability estimate without evidence about the underlying events.

limitations: A playful conjecture; no established probability principle supports it.

razors.name: Everyday razor
razors.summary: Frequent repetition can accumulate substantial output.
razors.body: Frequency can support habit and repeated feedback. Recovery, quality, and diminishing returns prevent a simple equation between repetition and improvement. Arithmetic about days of practice is not evidence of guaranteed compounded skill growth.
razors.lensQuestion: Would a sustainable increase in practice frequency improve cumulative progress?

examples.text: A learner replaces one irregular monthly session with brief, attentive daily practice.
examples.note: The potential benefit comes from useful practice and continuity, not a guaranteed mathematical growth rate.

limitations: Arithmetic about days of practice is not evidence of guaranteed compounded skill growth.

razors.name: Feynman razor
razors.summary: Clear explanation can expose gaps in understanding.
razors.body: A request for clarity can diagnose gaps in understanding. Some subjects still require prerequisites, notation, or substantial time even when the expert understands them well. Modern label; not a verified quotation or a test that every expert topic must be explainable to a child.
razors.lensQuestion: Can I explain the mechanism clearly without using jargon to hide a gap?

examples.text: A student repeats the word 'optimization' but cannot describe what is optimized or what changes.
examples.note: The explanation exposes a missing account of the objective and process, not merely unfamiliar vocabulary.

limitations: Modern label; not a verified quotation or a test that every expert topic must be explainable to a child.

razors.name: Gell-Mann razor
razors.summary: Retain skepticism about media reporting beyond your own expertise.
razors.body: Expertise makes some errors easier to detect, while unfamiliarity can conceal others. The response is source checking, not a presumption that every report is false. Related to Gell-Mann amnesia; not a quantified estimate of journalistic error.
razors.lensQuestion: Would I scrutinize this report as closely as a report about my own expertise?

examples.text: An engineer notices serious errors in a report about her field but assumes the adjacent economics report must be accurate.
examples.note: The contrast reveals inconsistent scrutiny; it does not prove the economics report is wrong.

limitations: Related to Gell-Mann amnesia; not a quantified estimate of journalistic error.

razors.name: Grice's razor
razors.summary: Avoid multiplying semantic meanings when pragmatic inference adequately explains the difference.
razors.body: An inferred conversational suggestion need not be part of a word's conventional meaning. Genuine lexical ambiguity still needs evidence and cannot be eliminated by stipulation. Do not conflate with the general principle of charity.
razors.lensQuestion: Can context and conversational inference explain the wording without adding another dictionary meaning?

examples.text: 'Some students passed' is taken to suggest that not all passed.
examples.note: The 'not all' suggestion can be a cancellable implicature: 'Some passed; in fact, all did.'

limitations: Do not conflate with the general principle of charity.

razors.name: Guillaume's razor
razors.summary: A linguistic parsimony principle associated with minimizing unnecessary semantic distinctions.
razors.body: This name circulates with varying linguistic formulations. It should not be treated as a universally standardized rule or as an exact synonym for every account of Gricean pragmatics. Sometimes identified with Grice's razor; attribution and formulation vary.
razors.lensQuestion: Is the apparent semantic distinction better explained by an independently motivated contextual process?

examples.text: A familiar word appears to convey a special implication only in one conversational setting.
examples.note: A contextual explanation may avoid inventing a new lexical sense for every setting.

limitations: Sometimes identified with Grice's razor; attribution and formulation vary.

razors.name: Hanlon's razor
razors.summary: Avoid inferring malice when error or incompetence adequately explains the behavior.
razors.body: Intent is an additional claim requiring support. The practical response to harm can remain firm even while the motive is uncertain. A defeasible heuristic, not evidence that malice never occurs.
razors.lensQuestion: Could error, missing information, or neglect explain this outcome without hostile intent?

examples.text: A colleague omits your name from an announcement, and you infer deliberate sabotage.
examples.note: An outdated template could explain the omission. Repeated documented exclusion would change the assessment.

limitations: A defeasible heuristic, not evidence that malice never occurs.

razors.name: Hitchens's razor
razors.summary: An unsupported assertion may be dismissed without proving its negation.
razors.body: The razor concerns the burden of supporting a claim. Rejecting the offered justification does not prove that the claim's negation is true. Withholding acceptance is distinct from establishing falsity.
razors.lensQuestion: What evidence has been offered for the assertion being made?

examples.text: Someone claims an invisible device controls your dreams but offers no observation that distinguishes this from ordinary dreaming.
examples.note: You can withhold acceptance without having to locate and disprove every possible device.

limitations: Withholding acceptance is distinct from establishing falsity.

razors.name: Hume's guillotine
razors.summary: A normative conclusion cannot follow from exclusively descriptive premises without a normative bridge.
razors.body: Facts can be indispensable to moral reasoning without supplying its entire normative basis. Adding an explicit value premise makes the missing commitment available for assessment. Listed with razors by convention; it is a constraint on inference rather than a parsimony heuristic.
razors.lensQuestion: Which normative premise connects the descriptive facts to the proposed obligation?

examples.text: Most employees work late; therefore every employee ought to work late.
examples.note: The conclusion needs a normative bridge explaining why common behavior creates an obligation.

limitations: Listed with razors by convention; it is a constraint on inference rather than a parsimony heuristic.

razors.name: Hume's razor
razors.summary: A proposed cause must have enough explanatory capacity to produce its assigned effect.
razors.body: The apparent size of a cause does not settle its causal capacity: a small trigger can release stored energy. Assess the whole mechanism rather than comparing appearances. Distinct from Hume's guillotine.
razors.lensQuestion: Does the proposed cause have the demonstrated capacity to produce this effect?

examples.text: A small desk fan is offered as the sole explanation for structural damage across a city.
examples.note: The account needs evidence of a mechanism with the relevant scale of causal power.

limitations: Distinct from Hume's guillotine.

razors.name: Instagram razor
razors.summary: Published images often reflect selection from many alternatives.
razors.body: A published image is a selected observation rather than a random sample of life. Selection can distort impressions without making the depicted moment entirely fabricated. The name does not imply a known number of rejected images.
razors.lensQuestion: What selection process produced this image or success story?

examples.text: A flawless travel photograph is presented as an ordinary moment of a trip.
examples.note: The frame may omit failed shots, staging, editing, or unpleasant surrounding events.

limitations: The name does not imply a known number of rejected images.

razors.name: Kant's counter-razor
razors.summary: Do not prematurely reduce the genuine variety of things.
razors.body: Economy should not eliminate real variety merely for convenience. The rule is a counterweight, not a demand to treat every superficial difference as fundamental. A restraint on unjustified simplification.
razors.lensQuestion: Am I erasing a genuine distinction before establishing that it is unnecessary?

examples.text: Two different measurement processes are assumed identical because merging them gives a shorter report.
examples.note: Independent evidence of their different error patterns is a reason to preserve the distinction.

limitations: A restraint on unjustified simplification.

razors.name: Luck razor
razors.summary: Consider options that increase exposure to useful opportunities.
razors.body: Some actions create more opportunities for beneficial encounters than others. Exposure also brings costs and risks, so more contact is not always better. Outcomes remain uncertain.
razors.lensQuestion: Which feasible choice exposes me to more useful, diverse opportunities?

examples.text: A researcher chooses between isolated browsing and an affordable interdisciplinary workshop relevant to her work.
examples.note: The workshop may increase useful contacts, but its cost and relevance still need assessment.

limitations: Outcomes remain uncertain.

razors.name: Menger's anti-razor
razors.summary: Do not use fewer explanatory resources than are necessary.
razors.body: Too little structure can mislead as much as too much structure. An adequate model can require several assumptions, variables, or mechanisms. A counterweight to excessive parsimony.
razors.lensQuestion: Is the simplest proposed account missing a resource required to explain the observations?

examples.text: A forecast drops all seasonal terms and consequently misses a repeated annual cycle.
examples.note: Seasonal structure is justified by the repeated pattern rather than gratuitous complication.

limitations: A counterweight to excessive parsimony.

razors.name: Narcissism razor
razors.summary: People may be less focused on you than you assume.
razors.body: People's attention is limited and often directed toward their own concerns. Some actions nevertheless receive sustained attention, so the advice must remain contextual. Not a diagnosis of narcissism.
razors.lensQuestion: What evidence shows that others are attending to this detail as intensely as I am?

examples.text: You assume everyone at a conference noticed a small stumble in your introduction.
examples.note: Other attendees may be preoccupied with their own presentations and conversations.

limitations: Not a diagnosis of narcissism.

razors.name: Naval's razor
razors.summary: For otherwise comparable options, consider the one with short-term difficulty and long-term benefits.
razors.body: This advice counters short-term avoidance in otherwise comparable choices. Pain can also signal a bad plan, and feasibility and downside risk still matter. Context-dependent decision advice, not a general rule to maximize pain.
razors.lensQuestion: Am I rejecting a durable benefit solely because its immediate cost is uncomfortable?

examples.text: Two training options have similar prospects, but one demands difficult foundational study before later benefits.
examples.note: Consider the delayed benefit without assuming that the more painful option is automatically better.

limitations: Context-dependent decision advice, not a general rule to maximize pain.

razors.name: Network razor
razors.summary: Connect people when the introduction is likely to benefit both.
razors.body: Connecting people can reduce search costs and open collaboration. Relevance, consent, and others' attention constrain when an introduction helps. General social advice rather than a rule of inference.
razors.lensQuestion: Would both people plausibly benefit from an introduction they are comfortable receiving?

examples.text: Two researchers separately mention complementary projects and welcome an introduction.
examples.note: A consented introduction could benefit both; sharing contact details without permission would change the case.

limitations: General social advice rather than a rule of inference.

razors.name: New-opportunity razor
razors.summary: Evaluate both the desired outcome and the work needed to reach it.
razors.body: An opportunity contains a process as well as an imagined reward. Assessing both can prevent commitment based only on a flattering outcome scenario. General decision advice, included because it circulates explicitly as a razor.
razors.lensQuestion: Do I value the likely outcome and accept the recurring work and downside needed to pursue it?

examples.text: A prospective founder likes the idea of owning a company but dislikes selling, hiring, and handling uncertainty.
examples.note: Considering the daily work reveals a mismatch concealed by the attractive end state.

limitations: General decision advice, included because it circulates explicitly as a razor.

razors.name: Occam's razor
razors.summary: Prefer fewer unnecessary assumptions between otherwise adequately supported explanations.
razors.body: Parsimony compares explanatory adequacy as well as assumption costs. A more complicated explanation can be preferable when it explains evidence the simpler one cannot. Does not establish that the simplest imaginable explanation is true.
razors.lensQuestion: Which account fits the evidence with the fewest unsupported assumptions?

examples.text: The printer stopped after its paper tray emptied. A second account proposes a hidden remote attack.
examples.note: Checking and refilling the empty tray tests an explanation with direct support; the attack requires additional evidence.

limitations: Does not establish that the simplest imaginable explanation is true.

razors.name: Opinion razor
razors.summary: Withhold firm opinions until sufficiently informed about the question and objections.
razors.body: Confidence should reflect the work and evidence behind a judgment. Practical decisions can still require provisional views under uncertainty. A popular epistemic maxim.
razors.lensQuestion: Do I understand enough of the evidence and objections to hold this view confidently?

examples.text: Someone asks for a firm position on a technical dispute you have only seen in a headline.
examples.note: Withholding judgment preserves the distinction between a first impression and an informed conclusion.

limitations: A popular epistemic maxim.

razors.name: Optimist razor
razors.summary: Consider the benefits of constructive, possibility-oriented collaborators.
razors.body: Possibility-oriented collaborators can make action and learning easier. Pessimistic warnings can also be accurate and should be judged on their reasons. Optimism does not guarantee accuracy or success.
razors.lensQuestion: Does this collaborator pair constructive possibilities with honest attention to constraints?

examples.text: One team member proposes testable ways forward while another dismisses every experiment without examining it.
examples.note: Constructive engagement can help the team act; uncritical optimism would still miss real risks.

limitations: Optimism does not guarantee accuracy or success.

razors.name: Popper's razor
razors.summary: A scientific theory should rule out possible observations and thus risk refutation.
razors.body: Falsifiability concerns a theory's exposure to potential counterevidence. Actual testing also depends on measurement, auxiliary assumptions, and the possibility of experimental error. A summary of Popper's contested demarcation proposal; falsifiability does not establish truth.
razors.lensQuestion: What possible observation would count against this theory?

examples.text: A prediction is revised after every outcome so that the theory always claims success.
examples.note: The account does not take a clear observational risk if every result is declared compatible afterward.

limitations: A summary of Popper's contested demarcation proposal; falsifiability does not establish truth.

razors.name: Pygmalion razor
razors.summary: Consider environments with constructive expectations for your development.
razors.body: Expectations can influence interaction, opportunities, and persistence. Their effects depend on context and should not be mistaken for control over another person's achievement. Not a guarantee that expectations determine achievement.
razors.lensQuestion: Does this environment combine constructive expectations with realistic support?

examples.text: A tutor expects a student to improve and supplies specific feedback and practice.
examples.note: The support can matter; pressure without resources or attainable goals is a different situation.

limitations: Not a guarantee that expectations determine achievement.

razors.name: Rand's conceptual razor
razors.summary: Do not create or merge concepts without a justified cognitive need.
razors.body: Conceptual economy concerns the justification of distinctions and integrations. It does not prohibit technical terms that capture a useful, previously unmarked difference. One of two different formulations circulated under Rand's razor.
razors.lensQuestion: Does this new category identify a distinction the inquiry genuinely needs?

examples.text: A database invents a separate basic kind for red, left-handed, Tuesday-born customers without a relevant purpose.
examples.note: The combination can be described without treating it as an explanatory kind.

limitations: One of two different formulations circulated under Rand's razor.

razors.name: Rand's primaries razor
razors.summary: Identify the fundamental premises on which the argument depends.
razors.body: Tracing an argument to its foundations exposes commitments that may otherwise remain hidden. It does not itself establish that the selected foundations are correct. Distinct from the conceptual-economy formulation.
razors.lensQuestion: Which basic premises must be accepted for this argument to work?

examples.text: A policy argument assumes, without stating it, that only aggregate income matters.
examples.note: Stating that premise allows disagreement about values to be separated from disagreement about predicted income.

limitations: Distinct from the conceptual-economy formulation.

razors.name: Room razor
razors.summary: Seek environments where other people can teach you.
razors.body: Learning often benefits from contact with people who know things one does not. An intimidating setting without support or relevance may be unhelpful. Advice about learning, not a measure of intelligence.
razors.lensQuestion: Will this setting expose me to useful knowledge and permit constructive participation?

examples.text: An experienced designer joins a workshop where others have deeper accessibility expertise.
examples.note: The learning opportunity comes from the relevant expertise and exchange, not from a global ranking of intelligence.

limitations: Advice about learning, not a measure of intelligence.

razors.name: Sagan standard
razors.summary: Claims with very low prior plausibility require particularly strong evidential support.
razors.body: A surprising claim can be established by ordinary methods when the evidence is sufficiently discriminating. Prior improbability is a reason to demand strength, not a license to ignore evidence. Extraordinary evidence means evidential strength, not necessarily an exotic kind of evidence.
razors.lensQuestion: How strongly does this evidence favor the claim over plausible alternatives?

examples.text: A blurry photograph is offered as proof of a previously unknown spacecraft.
examples.note: Camera artifacts and ordinary aircraft must be assessed before the image can carry the proposed evidential weight.

limitations: Extraordinary evidence means evidential strength, not necessarily an exotic kind of evidence.

razors.name: Smart-friends razor
razors.summary: Treat informed peers' unusual interests as leads for investigation.
razors.body: An informed peer can provide a valuable lead for investigation. Shared incentives and common sources can also generate correlated mistakes. Social agreement is not proof and can propagate shared error.
razors.lensQuestion: What do these informed people know, and are their reasons independent?

examples.text: Several colleagues investigate the same new tool, but all learned about it from one sponsored post.
examples.note: Their apparent agreement is not independent corroboration; inspect the underlying evidence.

limitations: Social agreement is not proof and can propagate shared error.

razors.name: Tarzwell's razor
razors.summary: Treat strong emotion as a reason to reassess confidence in judgment.
razors.body: Emotion can draw attention to real concerns while also changing confidence and interpretation. Calmness is not proof of correctness either. Popular attribution and formulation; not an independently verified empirical law.
razors.lensQuestion: Should I reassess this judgment after the immediate emotional surge subsides?

examples.text: After an angry meeting, you conclude a colleague's entire career is fraudulent.
examples.note: Delaying the global judgment permits the actual evidence to be assessed separately from anger.

limitations: Popular attribution and formulation; not an independently verified empirical law.
